prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth strip supports a coarse near-to-far layout: the leftmost views contain mostly mid/far shelving and room surfaces, while the camera wearer’s hand-held black object becomes very near (about 0.2–0.5 m) in the middle frames; the two standing people in the last two frames appear roughly 0.8–1.5 m ahead, with tables, chairs, and wall-mounted equipment behind or beside them at about 1–3 m. It makes depth ordering clearer than RGB, including the wearer’s hand/object in front of the floor and fixtures, the nearer edges of chairs and tables, and the people occluding the background; bright border fragments and foreground blobs also indicate objects partly outside the lower and right image boundaries. Across the five frames the viewpoint turns from shelving and floor toward the right side of the room, bringing a person into the center-right foreground and then another person into the far-right foreground, but exact approach or retreat is difficult to separate from camera rotation. The map is unreliable for metric distance, fine boundaries, and reflective or thin structures: several people and objects merge into pale blobs, large background regions have nearly uniform gray, and strong white edge areas likely exaggerate nearness.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map identifies a dog left of the wearer in an early frame, a partly visible person near the upper middle, a large person in front/right in the fourth frame, another person at the right in the fifth frame, plus chairs and a cup near the right-side work area. It clarifies object identity and separation where RGB is crowded: the dog is isolated from the dark floor/background, the people are distinguished from nearby furniture, and small chair/cup regions show their relative left/right placement; however, it provides no direct metric depth, so RGB and apparent size only suggest the dog and central small person are farther away (roughly 1–3 m) while the two large people are nearer (roughly 0.7–1.5 m). The large people face generally sideways rather than squarely toward the wearer, but facial blur and mask shape do not reliably establish gaze; chairs and the cup are near those people, while the wearer’s own hand/object is within about 0.5 m but is mostly not segmented. Across frames, labeled content shifts from the dog on the left to a partial person and then to larger people and furniture on the right as the camera turns; masks cut off at the top, bottom, and right edges reveal partial views, and the anomalous combined label near the upper middle, missed equipment, fragmented chairs, and absent hand-held object show unreliable classification and coverage.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black in all five frames, so it supplies no detected body or hand joints, orientations, reach geometry, or motion trajectory beyond what can be inferred from RGB. Consequently it cannot establish whether either visible person faces or looks toward the wearer, nor whether their hands reach the table, cup, chairs, equipment, or the wearer; RGB only supports coarse spatial observations that the wearer’s own hand/object is within arm’s reach and the standing people are approximately 0.7–1.5 m ahead/right. It also cannot resolve occluded or cropped limbs, including body parts outside the upper, lower, and right borders, or show whether people approach, retreat, or turn across the five frames. The total absence of skeletons despite clearly visible people and the wearer’s hands indicates detection failure, likely worsened by blur, cropping, occlusion, unusual egocentric perspective, and the panoramic distortion.
